title: A Technical Deep Dive Is Not a Crisis Response
author: Phil Hill
summary: Phil Hill's On EdTech newsletter analyzes Instructure's (Canvas LMS) handling of a recent cybersecurity incident, arguing that the company's 'Technical Deep Dive' webinar confirmed what he had previously diagnosed: the crisis is being managed as an engineering problem rather than a trust problem. The webinar featured technical staff and a CrowdStrike incident response lead, but conspicuously lacked senior leadership taking institutional accountability. Hill argues that the carefully lawyered format -- scripted responses, pre-selected questions, no live Q&A -- signals that the company's legal team is driving the response strategy. The technical content was genuine, but crisis communication requires naming accountability, not just demonstrating competence. Hill draws a contrast with Josh Coates's 2012 Canvas outage response, which featured direct executive acknowledgment of failure, as the model Instructure should be following.
points: * Crisis communication requires institutional accountability, not just technical transparency: showing competence without naming responsibility does not rebuild trust. * Instructure's webinar format -- scripted responses, pre-selected questions, technical staff only -- signals that the legal team is driving response strategy, which is visible and trust-eroding. * The absence of senior leadership from the webinar stage sends its own message: this is being treated as an engineering incident rather than an institutional failure. * A useful contrast: Josh Coates's 2012 Canvas outage response ('we are embarrassed, we are sorry, we will do better') combined technical accountability with executive ownership. * EdTech institutions occupy a special position of trust with educational clients; crisis responses that prioritize legal protection over institutional acknowledgment damage the relationship asymmetrically.
quotes: Yesterday's customer-focused "Technical Deep Dive on Recent Security Incident" webinar was the company's most substantive public-facing communication to date.
It also confirmed, in nearly every choice of format and phrasing, that the playbook has not changed.
The technical content was genuine, but the framing was lawyered and carefully read by script.
And the people on screen -- Chief Architect Zach Pendleton, CISO Steve Proud, and CrowdStrike incident response head James Perry -- were, conspicuously, still focused only on the technical platform.
## What Was on Screen The webinar ran roughly twenty-five minutes, with a same-day rerun and a next-morning replay for customers who could not attend live.
The short, tightly-produced format was itself the message: this is being handled as an engineering problem.
To Instructure's credit, the company was explicit up front about the scope it had chosen.
